Software Design: Architecture, Patterns & Frameworks

How do four students turn the requirements of Block 5 into a structure they can build in four weeks and change without breaking it? This class answers in five lessons: what makes a design good and how to measure it; how to choose and record an architecture; the principles behind well-built classes; the classic design patterns; and the framework that will run your code, with the diagrams that show a design to another engineer.

Lesson 1 — Design concepts and design quality

0:00–0:11 · 11 minutes · slides 1–11
By the end of this lesson you can: Define software design and the four elements of the design model; explain abstraction, modularity, information hiding and separation of concerns; define cohesion and coupling and measure them on a small design; define refactoring and say why tests make it safe.

In full: Design concepts and design quality: abstraction, modularity, information hiding, separation of concerns, cohesion and coupling, refactoring — and the design model

Today's question

slide 1

Good morning. Last Tuesday your team wrote down, in Block 5, what your product must do: the functional requirements, the five non-functional requirements, the use cases and the domain model. Today we answer the next question: how will the product be built, so that four people can write it in four weeks and change it without breaking it? That question is software design.

We take it in four steps. First, what makes a design good, and how to measure it. Second, the large structure of a system — its architecture. Third, the principles and the reusable solutions — design patterns — that professionals apply to classes. Fourth, the framework that will run your code, and the diagrams that show a design to another engineer.

This hour serves LO2 (Learning Outcome 2): apply design patterns and framework activities for software design. There is no new Block today; the Studio is coached time to finish Block 5, and teams that are done can write one design-pattern card and set up the code skeleton that Block 7 needs.

From requirements to design: the design model

slide 5
software design — The activity, and its result, that translates the requirements of a product into a model of the software — its structure, its data, its interfaces and its components — detailed enough to be built and tested, before the code is written.

Your textbook, Pressman and Maxim, 9th edition, chapter 9↗, builds the design model from the requirements model in four elements, usually drawn as a pyramid. At the base is the data/class design: the classes and data structures, which grow out of the domain model of Block 5. Above it is the architectural design: the large components and how they connect. Then the interface design: how the software talks to its users, to other systems and between its own components. At the top is the component-level design: the internal details of each component — its classes, operations and algorithms. A fifth element, deployment-level design, says on which machines and services the components run.

Three properties make a design good. It implements every explicit requirement and the implicit ones the stakeholders expect. It is readable: a programmer and a tester can work from it. And it gives a complete picture of the software — data, functions and behaviour — at the level of detail the next activity needs. The rest of this lesson gives you the concepts with which designers reach those properties.

→ The figure of this lesson shows this part: Figure 1.

Abstraction and modularity

slide 6
abstraction — Describing a part of a system by what it does and what it represents, while leaving out the details that do not matter at that level of description.

Designers work at several levels of abstraction. A procedural abstraction is a named sequence of instructions with a precise function: borrow an item names everything that happens when a member borrows a game, without listing the steps. A data abstraction is a named collection of data that describes an object: a Loan has a member, an item, a start date and a due date. At the next level down, the same names are refined into operations and attributes.

modularity — The division of software into separately named and addressable components, called modules, that are integrated to satisfy the requirements.

Why divide at all? Because a person can keep only a limited amount of detail in mind at once; one 3,000-line file cannot be understood, reviewed or tested as a whole. But division has a cost too: every boundary between modules is an interface that must be designed, documented and tested. Too few modules make each one hard to understand; too many make the integration effort grow. The aim is the middle: modules small enough to understand, few enough to integrate.

Information hiding and separation of concerns

slide 7
information hiding — A design principle stated by David Parnas in 1972: each module is designed around a decision that is likely to change, and hides that decision behind its interface, so that the other modules do not depend on it.

In his paper On the criteria to be used in decomposing systems into modules↗, Parnas compared two ways to divide the same program. The first followed the steps of the processing, one module per step. The second gave each module one design decision to hide — for example, how the data was stored. When a decision changed, the second design needed changes in one module; the first needed changes almost everywhere. The rule for you: when ClubLend sends reminders by e-mail, only one module should know that e-mail is used; the others ask it to remind a member.

separation of concerns — The principle that a complex problem is easier to solve when it is divided into parts — concerns — that can each be understood, solved and changed separately.

A concern is a feature or a behaviour named in the requirements: lending, reminding, reporting. Separation of concerns says each of them should be placed in its own part of the design. Information hiding says how to draw the boundary: around what is likely to change.

Cohesion and coupling

slide 8

Abstraction, modularity and information hiding lead to one goal that your textbook calls functional independence: modules that each do one clearly defined job and interact little with the others. Two measures, introduced by Stevens, Myers and Constantine in their 1974 article Structured design↗, express it.

cohesion — The degree to which the elements inside one module — its methods and data — belong together because they serve one purpose. High cohesion is the goal.
coupling — The degree to which one module depends on other modules: how many it uses, and how much it must know about them. Low coupling is the goal.

Remember the two words together: high cohesion, low coupling. A cohesive module can be understood and tested alone; a loosely coupled module can be changed without changing its neighbours.

Both can be measured. TCC (Tight Class Cohesion), defined by Bieman and Kang in 1995, takes every pair of methods of a class and counts the pairs that use at least one common attribute: TCC (Tight Class Cohesion) = linked pairs ÷ all pairs, from 0 to 1. A related check counts the islands of a class — the groups of methods connected by shared attributes; this is the idea behind the LCOM4 (Lack of Cohesion in Methods, version 4) metric. More than one island means the class does several unrelated jobs. For coupling, this course uses the coupling count: the number of other classes a class depends on.

→ The figure of this lesson shows this part: Figure 1.

Refactoring

slide 9
refactoring — A change to the internal structure of software that makes it easier to understand and cheaper to modify, without changing its observable behaviour (Martin Fowler, Refactoring).

Refactoring is how a design improves after the first version exists. Fowler's book↗ catalogues the moves: extract class when a class does two jobs, move method when a method uses another class's data more than its own, rename when a name hides the purpose, remove duplication when the same rule appears twice. Each move is small, and each is checked by running the tests that already exist — the red → green → refactor cycle you met in Class 4. Without tests, a change of structure is a guess.

Refactoring returns twice in this course: in Block 7, as the third step of Test-Driven Development, and in Class 10, as the main tool of preventive maintenance and the way a team pays back technical debt.

Check the answer

Cohesion: how strongly the parts of one module belong together (aim high). Coupling: how strongly one module depends on others (aim low). Modularity: division into separately named, addressable modules. Information hiding: each module hides a decision likely to change behind its interface.

Real-life example · Team Owl · ClubLend (fictional)

ClubLend: one class, three jobs — measured, split, measured again

slide 10
TaskTeam Owl (fictional) builds ClubLend, the lending app of a student club that lends board games and books. Its first design puts every method in one class, LoanDesk: searching the catalogue, borrowing and returning items, sending and previewing reminders, and building and exporting the monthly report. The team measures the cohesion and coupling of LoanDesk, splits it into one class per job, measures again, and checks what a change request costs in each design.
Relation to the lectureIt applies Lesson 1: modularity, information hiding, separation of concerns, high cohesion and low coupling — measured with TCC (Tight Class Cohesion), islands and the coupling count — and refactoring as a change of structure that keeps the behaviour.

The first design. LoanDesk has seven methods and depends on five other classes: Item, Loan, Member, EmailGateway and CsvFile. Of its 21 pairs of methods, only 5 share an attribute, so TCC (Tight Class Cohesion) = 5 ÷ 21 = 0.24. Its methods fall into three islands that share nothing: the loan methods (items, loans, members), the reminder methods (the reminder text and the e-mail gateway) and the report methods (the report lines and the file path). Three islands, three jobs, one class.

The refactoring. The team moves each island into its own class: LoanService (search the catalogue, borrow, return), Reminder (send and preview a reminder) and LoanReport (add a line, export the file). No behaviour changes — the same seven methods exist — so the tests written for the first design still pass. Each new class has TCC (Tight Class Cohesion) 1.00 and one island; the largest coupling count falls from 5 to 3. Information hiding appears at once: only Reminder knows that an e-mail gateway exists.

The effect on a change request. A change request arrives: send reminders by text message as well as by e-mail (CR-1 (Change Request 1)). In the first design it changes LoanDesk, and all seven of its methods must be re-tested. In the refactored design it changes Reminder only: two methods to re-test. The total number of dependencies rose from 5 to 7, because three classes now need some of the same classes; what improved is that no class depends on everything, and a change stays inside one small module.

# =============================================================================# CS 330 · Class 6 · Lesson 1 — Demo 1# ClubLend (Team Owl, fictional): cohesion and coupling before and after a refactoring## TASK. Team Owl describes its ClubLend design as data: for every class, the# methods it contains, the attributes each method reads or writes, and the other# classes the class depends on. The program measures three things for every class:#   - TCC (Tight Class Cohesion): the share of method pairs that use at least one#     common attribute (Bieman and Kang, 1995); 1.00 means every pair is linked;#   - islands: the number of groups of methods that are linked by shared#     attributes (the idea behind the LCOM4 metric of Hitz and Montazeri, 1995);#     more than one island means the class performs several unrelated jobs;#   - coupling count: the number of other classes the class depends on (lower is better).# It measures the original class LoanDesk, then the three classes of the# refactored design, and finally counts how many methods a change request# ("send reminders by text message as well as by e-mail") forces the team to re-test.## RELATION TO THE LECTURE. Lesson 1: modularity, information hiding, separation# of concerns, high cohesion and low coupling, and refactoring as a change of# structure that keeps the behaviour. The numbers printed here are the ones on# the lesson's slides and in Figure 1.## RUN IT: python3 demo1_clublend_cohesion_coupling.py   (any Python 3.8 or later, no extra package)# Educational material — Cyber.SoHo Educational Hub © 2026. All teams, products and people are fictional.# Use is governed by the Cyber.SoHo Legal Notice:# https://cyber-soho.github.io/prevmon/00.01.%20cyber.soho%20-%20legal.html# ============================================================================= # Import combinations(), which lists every unordered pair of items exactly once; the TCC formula works on pairs of methods.from itertools import combinations # BEFORE: the design as Team Owl first wrote it — one class, LoanDesk, holds every method of the product.before = {    # LoanDesk maps each method name to the set of attributes that the method reads or writes.    "LoanDesk": {        # search_catalogue reads the list of items to find the board games and books that match a query.        "search_catalogue": {"items"},        # borrow reads items and members and writes loans: it checks availability and records a new loan.        "borrow": {"items", "loans", "members"},        # return_item writes loans and items: it closes the loan and marks the item as available again.        "return_item": {"items", "loans"},        # send_reminder uses the e-mail gateway and the reminder text to contact a member.        "send_reminder": {"mail_gateway", "reminder_text"},        # preview_reminder shows the reminder text to a club officer before it is sent.        "preview_reminder": {"reminder_text"},        # add_report_row appends one line to the monthly report of the club.        "add_report_row": {"report_rows"},        # export_csv writes the report lines to a file at the configured path.        "export_csv": {"report_rows", "csv_path"},    # The closing brace ends the description of LoanDesk.    },# The closing brace ends the BEFORE design.} # The other classes each class of the BEFORE design depends on; their number is the coupling count.uses_before = {"LoanDesk": {"Item", "Loan", "Member", "EmailGateway", "CsvFile"}} # AFTER: the same seven methods, moved into three classes, one per job (separation of concerns).after = {    # LoanService keeps the catalogue and loan behaviour; its three methods share items and loans.    "LoanService": {"search_catalogue": {"items"}, "borrow": {"items", "loans", "members"}, "return_item": {"items", "loans"}},    # Reminder hides how a message travels (information hiding); both methods share the reminder text.    "Reminder": {"send_reminder": {"mail_gateway", "reminder_text"}, "preview_reminder": {"reminder_text"}},    # LoanReport builds and exports the monthly report; both methods share the report lines.    "LoanReport": {"add_report_row": {"report_rows"}, "export_csv": {"report_rows", "csv_path"}},# The closing brace ends the AFTER design.} # The dependencies of each AFTER class: each one now needs fewer other classes than LoanDesk did.uses_after = {"LoanService": {"Item", "Loan", "Member"}, "Reminder": {"Member", "EmailGateway"}, "LoanReport": {"Loan", "CsvFile"}}  # tcc() returns the share of method pairs that use at least one common attribute.def tcc(methods):    # Build the list of all unordered pairs of method names: n methods give n(n-1)/2 pairs.    pairs = list(combinations(methods, 2))    # A class with fewer than two methods has no pair to compare, so it is treated as fully cohesive.    if not pairs:        # Return 1.0, the highest possible value, for a class with zero or one method.        return 1.0    # Keep the pairs whose attribute sets intersect: the & operator returns the common attributes, and an empty set counts as false.    linked = [(a, b) for a, b in pairs if methods[a] & methods[b]]    # TCC is the number of linked pairs divided by the number of all pairs.    return len(linked) / len(pairs)  # islands() counts the groups of methods that are connected through shared attributes.def islands(methods):    # seen remembers every method that has already been placed in a group.    seen = set()    # count holds the number of groups found so far.    count = 0    # Try every method in turn as the possible start of a new group.    for start in methods:        # A method that already belongs to a group cannot start another one, so skip it.        if start in seen:            # continue jumps to the next method of the for loop.            continue        # An unvisited method starts a new group, so the counter grows by one.        count += 1        # The stack holds the methods of the current group whose neighbours are still to be checked.        stack = [start]        # Mark the starting method as placed in a group.        seen.add(start)        # Keep exploring while some method of the current group has unchecked neighbours.        while stack:            # Take the last method from the stack to examine its neighbours.            current = stack.pop()            # Compare it with every method of the class.            for other in methods:                # A method not yet placed that shares an attribute with the current one belongs to the same group.                if other not in seen and methods[current] & methods[other]:                    # Place the neighbour in the group.                    seen.add(other)                    # Push it on the stack so that its own neighbours are examined later.                    stack.append(other)    # After every method is placed, count is the number of separate groups.    return count  # report() prints one line of measurements for every class of a design.def report(label, design, uses):    # Visit each class with its dictionary of methods.    for cls, methods in design.items():        # Print the label, the class, its number of methods, TCC with two decimals, the islands and the coupling count.        print(f"{label} | {cls:<11} | methods {len(methods)} | TCC {tcc(methods):.2f} | islands {islands(methods)} | coupling {len(uses[cls])}")  # Measure the BEFORE design: one class with seven methods.report("before", before, uses_before)# Measure the AFTER design: three smaller classes.report("after ", after, uses_after) # The change request CR-1 asks for reminders by text message as well as by e-mail; it modifies send_reminder.changed_method = "send_reminder"# Compare the impact of CR-1 on the two designs.for label, design in (("before", before), ("after", after)):    # Find the class that owns the changed method: next() returns the first class whose methods include it.    owner = next(cls for cls, methods in design.items() if changed_method in methods)    # Every method of the changed class must be re-tested, because the change can affect any of them.    print(f"{label}: CR-1 'text-message reminders' changes {owner}; re-test {len(design[owner])} methods") # Step-by-step explanation
  1. The design is data: each class maps its method names to the set of attributes the method reads or writes. This is the question a reviewer asks of every method: which fields does it touch?
  2. tcc() lists every pair of methods with combinations() — 7 methods give 21 pairs — and keeps the pairs whose attribute sets intersect (the & operator). LoanDesk keeps 5 pairs: TCC (Tight Class Cohesion) = 5 ÷ 21 = 0.24.
  3. islands() starts from one method and follows shared attributes to every method it can reach, then starts again from a method not yet reached. LoanDesk needs three starts: loans, reminders, report — three islands.
  4. report() prints one line per class: number of methods, TCC (Tight Class Cohesion), islands and coupling count. Watch the visualisation: the method dots of LoanDesk fall into three coloured groups.
  5. The AFTER design contains the same seven methods in three classes. Each has TCC (Tight Class Cohesion) 1.00 and one island; the largest coupling count drops from 5 to 3.
  6. The last loop finds the class that owns send_reminder in each design with next() and prints how many methods must be re-tested when that class changes: 7 before, 2 after.

Flash-cards
Five flash-cards for Lesson 1 — click a card to turn it
software designclick to turn
The activity, and its result, that translates the requirements into a model of the software — structure, data, interfaces and components — detailed enough to be built and tested before the code is written.
information hidingclick to turn
Each module hides a design decision that is likely to change behind its interface, so other modules do not depend on that decision (David Parnas, 1972).
cohesionclick to turn
How strongly the elements inside one module belong together because they serve one purpose. Aim high. Measured, for example, by TCC (Tight Class Cohesion) = linked method pairs ÷ all method pairs.
couplingclick to turn
How strongly one module depends on other modules. Aim low. This course counts it as the number of other classes a class depends on (the coupling count).
refactoringclick to turn
A change to the internal structure of software that makes it easier to understand and cheaper to modify, without changing its observable behaviour; each small step is checked by the existing tests.

Lesson 2 — Architectural design
0:15–0:26 · 11 minutes · slides 13–20
By the end of this lesson you can: Define software architecture and an architectural style; describe six styles with their strengths and costs; choose a style from weighted decision drivers; record the decision in an ADR (Architecture Decision Record); check a design against the rule of the layered style.
In full: Architectural design: architectural styles — layered and 3-tier, MVC (Model–View–Controller), client–server, pipe-and-filter, event-driven, microservices — the architecture decision and its record


What software architecture is
slide 14



software architecture — The structure, or structures, of a system: its software elements, the externally visible properties of those elements, and the relationships among them (after Bass, Clements and Kazman, Software Architecture in Practice).


Architecture is the top of the design model: the few large parts of the system and how they connect — the browser, the web application, the database, the e-mail service. It is decided early and it is expensive to change late, because everything else is built inside it. That is why it fixes most of the quality attributes you wrote as non-functional requirements in Block 5: how fast the system answers, how easily it can be changed, how it can be tested and where it can be hosted.


One architecture can be shown in several views: a logical view (the components and their responsibilities), a deployment view (which machine or service runs each component), and others. The international standard ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010 (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission / Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers standard 42010)↗ describes how to document an architecture with views, each written for the concerns of particular stakeholders. For a student project, two drawings — one logical, one deployment — and one decision record are enough.


Architectural styles (1/2): layered and MVC (Model–View–Controller)
slide 15



architectural style — A named family of architectures that share a set of component types, a set of connector types (how components communicate), the constraints on how they may be combined, and a model of how the whole behaves.


A style is not a finished design; it is a pattern for the large structure that has been used many times, with known strengths and known costs. Six styles cover almost every student product, and many professional ones.


layered architecture — Components are grouped into layers; each layer offers services to the layer above it and uses only the services of the layer directly below it. The common three-tier form has a presentation layer, a business-logic layer and a data layer.


The rule of the layered style is a constraint you can check: a component may call only the layer directly below it (a strict layering), or any layer below it (a relaxed layering). The benefit: you can replace the data layer — a file today, a database tomorrow — without touching the presentation.


MVC (Model–View–Controller) — An architectural pattern that separates the Model (the data and the business rules), the View (what the user sees) and the Controller (what handles the user's input, updates the model and selects the view). Described by Trygve Reenskaug at Xerox PARC (Palo Alto Research Center) in 1978–79 for the Smalltalk system.


Web frameworks adapt MVC (Model–View–Controller) to the request–response cycle of the web. In Flask or Express, a route function plays the controller and a template the view; Django names its version MTV (Model–Template–View), because what it calls the view is the function that handles the request. The names change; the separation stays: data and rules in one place, display in another, input handling in a third.


→ The figure of this lesson shows this part: Figure 2.


Architectural styles (2/2): client–server, pipe-and-filter, event-driven, microservices
slide 16



client–server — Clients send requests over a network; a server provides the service and answers. The web is the best-known example: your browser is the client of the course's web application.


pipe-and-filter — Data flows through a chain of independent processing steps (filters) connected by channels (pipes); each filter reads its input, transforms it and writes its output, without knowing the other filters. Compilers and data-processing pipelines follow this style.


event-driven architecture — Components communicate by publishing events (“the order is ready”) and by reacting to the events they subscribe to, usually through a message broker; the producer of an event does not know which components consume it.


microservices — An architecture in which an application is a set of small services, each running in its own process, built around one business capability, deployed independently and communicating through lightweight mechanisms such as HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) (James Lewis and Martin Fowler, 2014).


Microservices let large organisations change and scale each capability independently. They also turn every call between parts into a network call that can fail, be slow or arrive twice, and they multiply the things to deploy and monitor. For a team of four in one semester, that cost is rarely worth paying: Fowler's own advice, MonolithFirst↗ (2015), is to start with one well-structured application and split it only when a real need appears. A layered application with MVC (Model–View–Controller) in its presentation layer is the usual first choice for a campus app — which is exactly what the example finds.


→ The figure of this lesson shows this part: Figure 2.


Choosing a style: drivers and trade-offs
slide 17



decision driver — A requirement, constraint or quality attribute that has a strong influence on an architecture decision — for example the response time under load, the skills of the team, or a free-hosting constraint.


No style is best in general; each trades one quality for another. Microservices give independent scaling at the cost of operational complexity; pipe-and-filter gives easy testing of each step at the cost of poor support for interaction. The engineer's job is to know which qualities matter for this product, and to make the trade-off visible.


A simple, honest tool is the weighted decision matrix. List the drivers and give each a weight, the weights adding up to 100. Score every candidate style from 1 to 5 on every driver. Multiply each score by its weight, add the products and divide by 100: the result stays on the 1-to-5 scale. The matrix does not make the decision for you — the scores remain your judgement — but it makes the judgement explicit, so that a teammate can disagree with one number instead of with the whole conclusion. Professional teams use heavier methods built on the same idea, such as the ATAM (Architecture Tradeoff Analysis Method) of the SEI (Software Engineering Institute). Public organisations formalise it further: the GC EAF (Government of Canada Enterprise Architecture Framework)↗ sets the criteria that federal review boards use to assess every digital initiative, in five layers — business, information, application, technology and security.


Recording the decision: the ADR (Architecture Decision Record)
slide 18



ADR (Architecture Decision Record) — A short document that records one architecture decision: its title, its status, the context that forced it, the decision itself and its consequences. Proposed by Michael Nygard in 2011; usually kept as numbered Markdown files in the repository.


You already wrote one: the process decision record of Block 3 follows the same form. Michael Nygard's original article↗ asks for five parts. The title names the decision ("ADR-001: architectural style of QueueLess"). The status says whether it is proposed, accepted or superseded. The context states the facts that force a decision, without opinions. The decision states what the team will do, in full sentences. The consequences list what becomes easier and what becomes harder. An accepted record is not edited later: when the team changes its mind, it writes a new record that supersedes the old one, so the history of the reasoning is kept. The community site adr.github.io↗ collects templates and tools.


Every architecture decision is shown with a diagram: boxes for the components, lines for the connectors, and a legend that says what the boxes and lines mean. A diagram without a legend can be read in several ways; with a legend, it can be checked.
👁 Active break — Visualize-it · 0:26–0:30 slide 21
Sketch your product's architecture
  1. Two minutes, alone, on paper: draw your product as boxes and lines — the browser, the application with its layers, the data store, any external service (e-mail, campus login).
  2. Add a three-line legend: what a box means, what a line means, what a dashed line means.
  3. One minute with a neighbour from another team: which style is it? Does any line skip a layer?
  4. Last minute: write the name of the style and one sentence of reason — the first line of a future ADR (Architecture Decision Record).
Check the answer
Most campus products end up layered, with MVC (Model–View–Controller) in the presentation layer, one database, and one or two external services. A line that goes from a view straight to the database skips the business layer — a violation of the layered rule.

Real-life example · Team Falcon · QueueLess (fictional)
QueueLess: five styles, five drivers, one decision record — and one layer violation
slide 19
TaskTeam Falcon (fictional) builds QueueLess, the cafeteria pre-order app: a student orders before the noon rush and picks up the order when the number is called; the kitchen sees the queue. The team takes five decision drivers from its Block 5 requirements and constraints, scores five candidate styles with a weighted matrix, records the decision as ADR-001, and checks its planned calls against the rule of the chosen style.
Relation to the lectureIt applies Lesson 2: architectural styles, decision drivers and their weights, the ADR (Architecture Decision Record), and the constraint that defines the layered style.
The drivers and their weights. Fit to a request–response interaction (25) — a student orders and waits for an answer; team skills (25); the free-hosting constraint of Block 5 (20); testability (15); and the noon-rush load (15): about 300 orders between 11:30 and 12:00, from the performance requirement.
The scores. Layered + MVC (Model–View–Controller) obtains (25×5 + 25×5 + 20×5 + 15×4 + 15×4) ÷ 100 = 4.70; client–server with a separate browser application 4.00; pipe-and-filter 3.25 — it fits batch processing, not an order form; event-driven 2.85; microservices 2.65 — strong on load, very weak on skills and free hosting. The team's ADR-001: Context — three or four students, one semester, free hosting, 300 orders in thirty minutes. Decision — one layered application with MVC (Model–View–Controller) in the presentation layer and one database. Consequences — one unit to deploy and test; every feature scales together; revisit if a second campus joins.
The rule, checked. The team lists its planned calls between components: order view → order controller → order service → order repository → database. One teammate proposes a shortcut: the kitchen screen reads the orders straight from the repository. The check finds it: the kitchen view (layer 1) calling the repository (layer 3) skips the business layer, so the kitchen screen would bypass the business rule of functional requirement FR-07 — the kitchen list shows only the orders the cashier has marked as paid, oldest first. The team routes the kitchen screen through the order service.

# =============================================================================# CS 330 · Class 6 · Lesson 2 — Demo 2# QueueLess (Team Falcon, fictional): choosing an architectural style, recording# the decision, and checking the rule of the chosen style## TASK. Team Falcon builds QueueLess, a cafeteria pre-order app. The team scores# five candidate architectural styles against five decision drivers taken from# its Block 5 requirements and constraints. Each driver has a weight (the weights# add up to 100) and each style receives a score from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent)# on each driver. The program computes the weighted score of every style# (sum of weight x score, divided by 100), ranks the styles, prints the short# Architecture Decision Record (ADR) for the winner, and then checks a list of# planned calls between components against the rule of a strict layered# architecture: a component may call only a component of the layer directly below.## RELATION TO THE LECTURE. Lesson 2: architectural styles, the drivers of an# architecture decision, the ADR (context, decision, consequences) and the# constraint that defines the layered style.## RUN IT: python3 demo2_queueless_architecture_decision.py   (Python 3.8 or later, no extra package)# Educational material — Cyber.SoHo Educational Hub © 2026. All teams, products and people are fictional.# Use is governed by the Cyber.SoHo Legal Notice:# https://cyber-soho.github.io/prevmon/00.01.%20cyber.soho%20-%20legal.html# ============================================================================= # The decision drivers and their weights; the five weights add up to 100, so each one is a percentage of importance.drivers = {"fit to request-response": 25, "team skills": 25, "free hosting": 20, "testability": 15, "noon-rush load": 15} # The five candidate styles; each one maps every driver to a score from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent).styles = {    # One deployable application in three layers, with MVC (Model-View-Controller) in the presentation layer.    "Layered + MVC (Model-View-Controller)": {"fit to request-response": 5, "team skills": 5, "free hosting": 5, "testability": 4, "noon-rush load": 4},    # A separate browser front end (the client) that calls one web interface on a server.    "Client-server": {"fit to request-response": 5, "team skills": 3, "free hosting": 4, "testability": 4, "noon-rush load": 4},    # A chain of processing steps, each reading the output of the previous one.    "Pipe-and-filter": {"fit to request-response": 1, "team skills": 4, "free hosting": 4, "testability": 5, "noon-rush load": 3},    # Components that publish and consume events through a message broker.    "Event-driven": {"fit to request-response": 3, "team skills": 2, "free hosting": 2, "testability": 3, "noon-rush load": 5},    # Many small services, each deployed and scaled on its own.    "Microservices": {"fit to request-response": 4, "team skills": 1, "free hosting": 1, "testability": 3, "noon-rush load": 5},# The closing brace ends the table of candidate styles.} # results will map each style to its weighted score.results = {}# Compute the weighted score of every style.for style, scores in styles.items():    # Multiply each score by the weight of its driver and add the products: this is the weighted sum.    total = sum(drivers[d] * scores[d] for d in drivers)    # Divide by 100 so that the result stays on the 1-to-5 scale of the scores.    results[style] = total / 100 # Sort the styles from the highest to the lowest weighted score.ranking = sorted(results.items(), key=lambda item: item[1], reverse=True)# Print the ranking, one style per line, with its position.for position, (style, score) in enumerate(ranking, start=1):    # The format :.2f shows the score with two decimals.    print(f"{position}. {style:<38} weighted score {score:.2f}") # The first entry of the ranking is the chosen style.chosen = ranking[0][0]# Print the ADR (Architecture Decision Record) in its usual parts: title, status, context, decision, consequences.print("Architecture Decision Record ADR-001: architectural style of QueueLess | status: accepted")# The context states the facts that make the decision necessary.print("Context: 3-4 students, one semester, free hosting, about 300 orders between 11:30 and 12:00")# The decision names the style and the difference with the runner-up.print(f"Decision: {chosen} ({ranking[0][1]:.2f} against {ranking[1][1]:.2f} for {ranking[1][0]})")# The consequences state both what the team gains and what it gives up.print("Consequences: one deployable unit and one database; every feature scales together; revisit if a second campus joins") # The layers of the chosen style, from the top (closest to the user) to the bottom (closest to the data).layers = {"OrderView": 1, "KitchenView": 1, "OrderController": 1, "OrderService": 2, "OrderRepository": 3, "Database": 4}# The planned calls between components, written as (caller, callee) pairs.calls = [    # The order form passes the student's input to its controller, inside the presentation layer.    ("OrderView", "OrderController"),    # The controller asks the business layer to place the order.    ("OrderController", "OrderService"),    # The service asks the data-access layer to store the order.    ("OrderService", "OrderRepository"),    # The repository writes to the database.    ("OrderRepository", "Database"),    # A shortcut proposed by one teammate: the kitchen screen reads orders directly from the repository.    ("KitchenView", "OrderRepository"),# The closing bracket ends the list of planned calls.]# Check every planned call against the rule of the strict layered style.for caller, callee in calls:    # The step is the number of layers between the caller and the callee.    step = layers[callee] - layers[caller]    # A call inside the same layer (step 0) or to the next layer down (step 1) respects the rule.    verdict = "ok" if step in (0, 1) else "VIOLATION: skips a layer"    # Print the call with its layers and the verdict.    print(f"{caller} (layer {layers[caller]}) -> {callee} (layer {layers[callee]}): {verdict}") # =============================================================================# STEP-BY-STEP EXPLANATION# 1. drivers holds the five drivers of the decision with their weights. They#    come from Block 5: request-response fit (the user places an order and#    waits for an answer), team skills, the free-hosting constraint,#    testability and the noon-rush load (a performance requirement).# 2. styles holds one row per candidate with a score from 1 to 5 per driver.#    The scores are the team's judgement; the program only makes the#    arithmetic and the ranking explicit and repeatable.# 3. The weighted sum: Layered + MVC = (25x5 + 25x5 + 20x5 + 15x4 + 15x4) / 100#    = 470 / 100 = 4.70. The other styles: client-server 4.00,#    pipe-and-filter 3.25, event-driven 2.85, microservices 2.65.# 4. sorted(..., reverse=True) ranks the styles; the first one is chosen.# 5. The ADR (Architecture Decision Record) records the decision in four parts: context (facts), decision#    (the chosen style and its margin), consequences (gains and costs), and#    the condition under which the team will revisit it.# 6. The layered style is defined by a rule: each layer calls only the layer#    directly below it. The check finds that KitchenView (layer 1) calling#    OrderRepository (layer 3) skips the business layer, so the kitchen screen#    would bypass the business rules. The team routes the kitchen screen#    through OrderService instead.# =============================================================================

Live visualisation of the lecture idea
Step-by-step explanation
  1. drivers maps each driver to its weight; the five weights add up to 100, so each one reads as a percentage of importance.
  2. styles holds one row per candidate with a score from 1 to 5 per driver — the team's judgement, written down.
  3. The first loop computes each weighted score with a generator expression inside sum() and divides by 100. Watch the bars grow in the visualisation, one style at a time.
  4. sorted(..., reverse=True) ranks the styles; the first entry is the decision, printed as ADR-001 with its context and consequences.
  5. layers gives each component its layer number; calls lists the planned calls as (caller, callee) pairs.
  6. The last loop computes the difference of layers for each call: 0 or 1 respects the strict rule; 2 or more skips a layer. KitchenView → OrderRepository is flagged.

software architectureclick to turn

architectural styleclick to turn

Lesson 3 — Object-oriented design principles
0:30–0:35 · 5 minutes · slides 22–27
By the end of this lesson you can: State the five SOLID (Single responsibility, Open–closed, Liskov substitution, Interface segregation, Dependency inversion) principles and DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself), KISS (Keep It Simple, Stupid) and YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It) in one sentence each; recognise a violation of each in a small design; explain how each principle lowers the cost of a change.
In full: Object-oriented design principles: SOLID (Single responsibility, Open–closed, Liskov substitution, Interface segregation, Dependency inversion) — SRP (Single Responsibility Principle), OCP (Open–Closed Principle), LSP (Liskov Substitution Principle), ISP (Interface Segregation Principle), DIP (Dependency Inversion Principle) — and DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself), KISS (Keep It Simple, Stupid), YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It)


SRP (Single Responsibility Principle) and OCP (Open–Closed Principle)
slide 23



Inside one component, classes depend on each other, and the way they depend decides how much a change costs. Five principles, collected by Robert C. Martin around 2000 and remembered by the acronym SOLID (Single responsibility, Open–closed, Liskov substitution, Interface segregation, Dependency inversion) that Michael Feathers proposed, describe dependencies that keep changes cheap. Each fits in one sentence.


SRP (Single Responsibility Principle) — A module should be responsible to one, and only one, actor — the person or group who asks for changes to it. Said differently: a class should have one reason to change (Robert C. Martin).


Martin's own wording, in a 2014 article↗, puts people at the centre: if the coach, the designer and the operations staff can all ask for changes to the same class, their changes collide in that class.


OCP (Open–Closed Principle) — Software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification: new behaviour is added by adding code, not by editing code that already works (Bertrand Meyer, 1988).


The usual sign of a violation is an if/elif chain on a kind or a format that must be edited every time a new kind appears. The usual cure is an interface with one implementation per kind.


LSP (Liskov Substitution Principle), ISP (Interface Segregation Principle) and DIP (Dependency Inversion Principle)
slide 24



LSP (Liskov Substitution Principle) — Objects of a subtype must be usable wherever objects of the parent type are expected, without changing the correct behaviour of the program: a subtype may not demand more (stronger preconditions) or promise less (weaker postconditions) than its parent (Barbara Liskov and Jeannette Wing, 1994).


A subclass that throws an error on an operation its parent offers breaks every program written for the parent. Liskov and Wing's article A behavioral notion of subtyping↗ gives the formal rules.


ISP (Interface Segregation Principle) — No client should be forced to depend on methods it does not use: several small interfaces, each made for one kind of client, are better than one large interface.


DIP (Dependency Inversion Principle) — High-level modules, which hold the policy of the product, should not depend on low-level modules, which hold the details; both should depend on abstractions — interfaces — and the details should implement those abstractions.


DIP (Dependency Inversion Principle) is why a well-designed class can be tested alone: in Block 7 you will replace the real e-mail sender by a small fake object that implements the same interface — a stub or a mock, a word of Class 7.


DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself), KISS (Keep It Simple, Stupid) and YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It)
slide 25



DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) — Every piece of knowledge — a business rule, a formula, a format — must have a single, unambiguous, authoritative representation within a system (Andrew Hunt and David Thomas, The Pragmatic Programmer, 1999).


KISS (Keep It Simple, Stupid) — Prefer the simplest design that meets the requirements; complexity must be justified by a requirement, not by elegance.


YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It) — Implement a capability when a requirement actually needs it, not when you foresee that it might; a rule from Extreme Programming.


Your Block 5 traceability matrix is the tool that applies YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It): a class or a feature with no requirement behind it is speculative work, and its cost is real — code to write, test and maintain. Two of these principles can be checked by a program; KISS (Keep It Simple, Stupid) is a judgement that people make in a review.

Real-life example · Team Wren · HabitHub (fictional)
HabitHub: a design review with eight findings — and a refactored design with none
slide 26
TaskTeam Wren (fictional) builds HabitHub: students track daily habits and streaks, and a weekly report shows what held and what slipped. Before writing the code of the weekly report, the team reviews its first design draft against SOLID (Single responsibility, Open–closed, Liskov substitution, Interface segregation, Dependency inversion), DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) and YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It), writing each principle as a rule that a reviewer — or a short program — can apply, and then reviews the refactored design.
Relation to the lectureIt applies Lesson 3: each principle stated as a checkable rule, a violation of each found in one small design, and the refactoring that removes it.
The draft. One class, WeeklyReport, computes the streaks (asked for by the habit coach), lays out the report (the designer) and sends it by e-mail (the operations person): three actors, an SRP (Single Responsibility Principle) finding. It chooses the output with an if/elif chain on the format, HTML (HyperText Markup Language) or PDF (Portable Document Format): an OCP (Open–Closed Principle) finding. It calls the e-mail server class and the template class directly: a DIP (Dependency Inversion Principle) finding. ArchivedHabit is a subclass of Habit that raises an error when check_in() is called: an LSP (Liskov Substitution Principle) finding. HabitStore is one interface of four methods, but the report uses only load() and the settings page only save() and delete(): two ISP (Interface Segregation Principle) findings. BadgeEngine repeats the streak rule (DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself)) and no requirement asks for badges (YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It)). Eight findings.
The refactoring. StreakCalculator owns the streak rule and answers to the coach. ReportFormatter is an interface; HtmlFormatter and PdfFormatter implement it, so a new format is a new class. Notifier is an interface; EmailNotifier implements it and hides the e-mail server. WeeklyReport only assembles the report from the three abstractions. Archived becomes a status of Habit, not a subclass. HabitStore is split into HabitReader (load) and HabitWriter (save, delete); export_xml, which no client used, is removed. BadgeEngine is parked until a requirement asks for it. The same review finds nothing.
What the review cannot do. KISS (Keep It Simple, Stupid) has no rule a program can apply; the team asks it as a question at the end of the review: is there a simpler design that meets FR-06, the weekly report? The answer was the refactored design — fewer lines per class, and no code without a requirement behind it.

# =============================================================================# CS 330 · Class 6 · Lesson 3 — Demo 3# HabitHub (Team Wren, fictional): a design review that applies SOLID, DRY and YAGNI as rules## TASK. Team Wren describes two versions of the HabitHub design as data: the# first draft and the refactored design. For every class the description lists# the actor (the person or group) who asks for changes to each responsibility,# the dependencies (marked "detail" when they are low-level mechanisms such as# an e-mail server or a file template, "abstraction" when they are interfaces),# whether the class contains a type switch (an if/elif chain on a kind or a# format), the operations a subclass refuses, the methods of an interface and the# methods each client uses, the requirement the class is traced to, and the# business rules it implements. The program applies one rule per principle and# prints every finding, first for the draft, then for the refactored design.## RELATION TO THE LECTURE. Lesson 3: SOLID — Single responsibility, Open-closed,# Liskov substitution, Interface segregation, Dependency inversion — and DRY# (Don't Repeat Yourself) and YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It). KISS (Keep It# Simple, Stupid) is listed too, but no program can judge simplicity for you.## RUN IT: python3 demo3_habithub_solid_check.py   (Python 3.8 or later, no extra package)# Educational material — Cyber.SoHo Educational Hub © 2026. All teams, products and people are fictional.# Use is governed by the Cyber.SoHo Legal Notice:# https://cyber-soho.github.io/prevmon/00.01.%20cyber.soho%20-%20legal.html# ============================================================================= # DRAFT: the first design of HabitHub's weekly report, described as data.draft = {    # WeeklyReport computes the streaks, lays out the page and sends it: three responsibilities.    "WeeklyReport": {        # Each responsibility is mapped to the actor who requests changes to it.        "responsibilities": {"compute weekly streaks": "coach", "lay out the report": "designer", "send the report": "operations"},        # It calls the e-mail server class and the HTML template class directly: both are low-level details.        "depends_on": {"SmtpMailer": "detail", "HtmlTemplate": "detail"},        # Its code chooses the output with if fmt == "html" ... elif fmt == "pdf": a type switch.        "type_switch": True,        # It implements the streak rule (consecutive days with a check-in) itself.        "rules": ["streak rule"],        # It is traced to the functional requirement FR-06 (weekly report).        "traced_to": ["FR-06"],    # The closing brace ends WeeklyReport.    },    # ArchivedHabit is declared as a subclass of Habit.    "ArchivedHabit": {        # The parent class whose objects it claims to be able to replace.        "parent": "Habit",        # Its check_in() method raises an error, so it refuses an operation that every Habit offers.        "refuses": ["check_in"],        # It is traced to FR-03 (archive a habit).        "traced_to": ["FR-03"],    # The closing brace ends ArchivedHabit.    },    # HabitStore is one interface that every part of the app must depend on.    "HabitStore": {        # The four methods that the interface declares.        "methods": ["load", "save", "delete", "export_xml"],        # The methods that each client really calls.        "clients": {"WeeklyReport": ["load"], "SettingsPage": ["save", "delete"]},        # It is traced to FR-01 (store my habits).        "traced_to": ["FR-01"],    # The closing brace ends HabitStore.    },    # BadgeEngine awards badges for long streaks; one teammate added it because it "might be fun".    "BadgeEngine": {        # It repeats the streak rule that WeeklyReport already implements.        "rules": ["streak rule"],        # No requirement of Block 5 asks for badges, so the list of traced requirements is empty.        "traced_to": [],    # The closing brace ends BadgeEngine.    },# The closing brace ends the draft design.} # REFACTORED: each class now has one responsibility, one actor, and depends on abstractions.refactored = {    # StreakCalculator owns the streak rule and answers to the coach only.    "StreakCalculator": {"responsibilities": {"compute weekly streaks": "coach"}, "depends_on": {"HabitReader": "abstraction"}, "rules": ["streak rule"], "traced_to": ["FR-06"]},    # ReportFormatter is an interface; HtmlFormatter and PdfFormatter implement it, so a new format is a new class.    "ReportFormatter": {"responsibilities": {"lay out the report": "designer"}, "traced_to": ["FR-06"]},    # Notifier is an interface; EmailNotifier implements it and hides the e-mail server.    "Notifier": {"responsibilities": {"send the report": "operations"}, "traced_to": ["FR-06"]},    # WeeklyReport now only assembles the report from the three abstractions.    "WeeklyReport": {"responsibilities": {"assemble the weekly report": "coach"}, "depends_on": {"StreakCalculator": "policy", "ReportFormatter": "abstraction", "Notifier": "abstraction"}, "traced_to": ["FR-06"]},    # An archived habit is now a Habit whose status is "archived"; no subclass refuses an inherited operation.    "Habit": {"responsibilities": {"store a habit, its status and its check-ins": "student"}, "traced_to": ["FR-01", "FR-03"]},    # HabitReader is a small interface with the one method that readers need.    "HabitReader": {"methods": ["load"], "clients": {"StreakCalculator": ["load"]}, "traced_to": ["FR-01"]},    # HabitWriter is a small interface with the two methods that the settings page needs; export_xml was removed.    "HabitWriter": {"methods": ["save", "delete"], "clients": {"SettingsPage": ["save", "delete"]}, "traced_to": ["FR-01"]},# The closing brace ends the refactored design; BadgeEngine is parked until a requirement asks for it.}  # review() applies one rule per principle to every class and returns the list of findings.def review(design):    # findings collects (principle, class, explanation) triples.    findings = []    # where maps each business rule to the classes that implement it, for the DRY check.    where = {}    # Examine each class with its description.    for name, c in design.items():        # SRP: the distinct actors behind the responsibilities of the class.        actors = sorted(set(c.get("responsibilities", {}).values()))        # More than one actor means more than one reason to change.        if len(actors) > 1:            # Record the finding with the names of the actors.            findings.append(("SRP", name, f"answers to {len(actors)} actors: {', '.join(actors)}"))        # OCP: a type switch must be edited every time a new kind is added.        if c.get("type_switch"):            # Record the finding.            findings.append(("OCP", name, "a new format means editing an if/elif chain"))        # LSP: a subclass that refuses an inherited operation cannot replace its parent.        if c.get("refuses"):            # Record the finding with the parent and the refused operations.            findings.append(("LSP", name, f"cannot replace {c['parent']}: refuses {', '.join(c['refuses'])}"))        # ISP: compare the methods of an interface with the methods each client really uses.        for client, used in c.get("clients", {}).items():            # The methods the client depends on without calling them.            unused = [m for m in c["methods"] if m not in used]            # Any unused method forces the client to depend on more than it needs.            if unused:                # Record the finding with the client and the unused methods.                findings.append(("ISP", name, f"{client} depends on {len(unused)} methods it never calls ({', '.join(unused)})"))        # DIP: the dependencies of the class that are low-level details.        details = [d for d, kind in c.get("depends_on", {}).items() if kind == "detail"]        # A class that depends on details instead of abstractions breaks the dependency inversion principle.        if details:            # Record the finding with the names of the details.            findings.append(("DIP", name, f"depends on low-level details: {', '.join(details)}"))        # YAGNI: a class that no requirement asks for is speculative work.        if "traced_to" in c and not c["traced_to"]:            # Record the finding.            findings.append(("YAGNI", name, "no requirement is traced to it"))        # DRY: remember which classes implement each business rule.        for rule in c.get("rules", []):            # setdefault creates the list the first time a rule is seen, then the class is appended.            where.setdefault(rule, []).append(name)    # After the loop, a rule implemented in more than one class is repeated knowledge.    for rule, owners in where.items():        # More than one owner breaks DRY: a change to the rule must be made in several places.        if len(owners) > 1:            # Record the finding with the classes that repeat the rule.            findings.append(("DRY", " + ".join(owners), f"the {rule} is implemented {len(owners)} times"))    # Return every finding to the caller.    return findings  # Review the two designs one after the other.for label, design in (("draft", draft), ("refactored", refactored)):    # Compute the findings of this design.    found = review(design)    # Print a heading with the number of findings.    print(f"{label}: {len(found)} findings")    # Print each finding on its own line.    for principle, where_found, why in found:        # Align the principle names so the list is easy to read.        print(f"  {principle:<5} {where_found:<26} {why}")# KISS is a judgement about simplicity that the team makes in the review meeting, not a rule a program can apply.print("KISS: judged by people in the review, not by this program") # =============================================================================# STEP-BY-STEP EXPLANATION# 1. Each design is data. The fields are the questions a reviewer asks: who#    asks for changes to this responsibility? what does the class depend on?#    is there an if/elif chain on a kind? does a subclass refuse an inherited#    operation? which interface methods does each client call? which#    requirement is the class for? which business rule does it implement?# 2. SRP (Robert C. Martin: a module should be responsible to one, and only#    one, actor): WeeklyReport answers to the coach, the designer and the#    operations person — three reasons to change.# 3. OCP: the if/elif chain on the format must be edited for every new format;#    after the refactoring, a new format is a new class that implements#    ReportFormatter, and no existing code is edited.# 4. LSP: ArchivedHabit raises an error on check_in, so a program written for#    any Habit breaks when it receives an archived one. The fix makes#    "archived" a status of Habit, not a subclass.# 5. ISP: HabitStore forces WeeklyReport to depend on save, delete and#    export_xml, which it never calls. Two small interfaces, HabitReader and#    HabitWriter, remove the unused dependencies.# 6. DIP: WeeklyReport depended on the e-mail server and the HTML template;#    after the refactoring it depends on the Notifier and ReportFormatter#    interfaces, and the details implement those interfaces.# 7. DRY and YAGNI: the streak rule existed twice, once in BadgeEngine, which#    no requirement asked for. Parking BadgeEngine removes both findings.# 8. The draft gives 8 findings; the refactored design gives 0. KISS stays a#    human judgement — a program can only check what can be written as a rule.# =============================================================================

Live visualisation of the lecture idea
Step-by-step explanation
  1. Each class is a dictionary of the facts a reviewer needs. The draft has four classes; the refactored design has seven smaller ones.
  2. review() visits every class. SRP (Single Responsibility Principle): it collects the distinct actors behind the responsibilities; more than one is a finding.
  3. OCP (Open–Closed Principle) and LSP (Liskov Substitution Principle) are read directly from the description: a type switch, or a subclass that refuses an inherited operation.
  4. ISP (Interface Segregation Principle): for each client of an interface, the program lists the methods it never calls; any unused method is a finding. DIP (Dependency Inversion Principle): any dependency marked “detail” is a finding.
  5. YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It): a class with an empty list of traced requirements. DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself): setdefault() builds a map from each business rule to the classes that implement it; a rule with two owners is a finding.
  6. The final loop reviews both designs: 8 findings for the draft, 0 for the refactored design. The last line states the limit: KISS (Keep It Simple, Stupid) is judged by people.

Flash-cards
Five flash-cards for Lesson 3 — click a card to turn it
SRP (Single Responsibility Principle)click to turn
A module should be responsible to one, and only one, actor — one reason to change. Violated when, for example, the coach, the designer and the operations staff all ask for changes to the same class.
OCP (Open–Closed Principle)click to turn
Open for extension, closed for modification: add a new kind by adding a class that implements an interface, not by editing an if/elif chain (Meyer, 1988).
LSP (Liskov Substitution Principle)click to turn
A subtype must be usable wherever its parent is expected, without breaking correct behaviour: no stronger preconditions, no weaker postconditions (Liskov and Wing, 1994).
DIP (Dependency Inversion Principle)click to turn
High-level policy and low-level details both depend on abstractions; the details implement the interfaces. It is what makes a class testable with stubs and mocks.
DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) and YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It)click to turn
DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself): every piece of knowledge has one authoritative representation (Hunt and Thomas, 1999). YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It): build a feature when a requirement needs it, not when you foresee it.

Question 1 · MCQ (multiple-choice question — one correct answer)
A class Invoice computes totals (asked for by accounting), formats the page (asked for by marketing) and saves to the database (asked for by operations). Which principle does it break first?

Question 2 · MCQ (multiple-choice question — one correct answer)
Every new export format requires a new branch in an if/elif chain inside ReportService. Which principle does this break?
Hint: Existing code must be edited to add a new kind.
Question 3 · MCQ (multiple-choice question — one correct answer)
ReadOnlyFile is a subclass of File, but its write() method raises an error. Which principle does it break?
Hint: Can a ReadOnlyFile be used everywhere a File is expected?
Question 4 · MCQ (multiple-choice question — one correct answer)
In the HabitHub review, why did BadgeEngine produce a YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It) finding?
Hint: Look at its traced requirements.
Question 5 · MSQ (multiple-select question — several correct answers)
Which changes apply the dependency inversion principle? (2 correct answers)
Hint: Policy and details should both depend on an abstraction.
Question 6 · MSQ (multiple-select question — several correct answers)
Which statements match ISP (Interface Segregation Principle), DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) or KISS (Keep It Simple, Stupid)? (3 correct answers)
Hint: One statement per principle is correct; the others twist them.

Lesson 4 — Design patterns
0:35–0:41 · 6 minutes · slides 28–35
By the end of this lesson you can: Define a design pattern by its problem, solution and consequences; state the intent of nine GoF (Gang of Four — Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides) patterns and recognise them in short scenarios; describe the structure of Observer and Strategy; choose a pattern from a problem and record it on a pattern card.
In full: Design patterns of the GoF (Gang of Four — Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides): creational (Singleton, Factory Method, Builder), structural (Adapter, Facade, Decorator), behavioural (Observer, Strategy, Command) — problem, solution, consequences, and how to choose


What a design pattern is
slide 29



design pattern — A named description of a design problem that occurs again and again in a given context, of the core of a solution to it — the roles of the classes and how they collaborate — and of the consequences of applying that solution.


The idea came from building architecture: Christopher Alexander described, in 1977, patterns for towns and houses — each a recurring problem with the core of a solution that can be reused many times without ever being built the same way twice. In 1994, Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson and John Vlissides — known as the GoF (Gang of Four — Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides) — applied it to object-oriented software in Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software↗, with 23 patterns in three families: creational patterns (how objects are created), structural patterns (how classes and objects are composed into larger structures) and behavioural patterns (how objects interact and divide the work).


A pattern always has three parts, and the third is the one beginners forget. The problem says when to use it. The solution names the participating classes and their collaboration — not code, but roles. The consequences say what the pattern costs: more classes, an extra level of indirection, sometimes a performance price.


Nine patterns you will meet (1/2): creational and structural
slide 30



FamilyPatternIntent, in one lineWhere in a campus app
CreationalSingletonGuarantee that a class has exactly one instance and give one global point of access to it.The configuration of the app, read once
CreationalFactory MethodDeclare an operation that creates an object, and let subclasses decide which concrete class to create.A report of the right type for each request
CreationalBuilderSeparate the step-by-step construction of a complex object from its representation, so one process can build different results.The weekly report, assembled section by section
StructuralAdapterConvert the interface of an existing class into the interface the client expects.Wrap the campus login library behind your own interface
StructuralFacadeProvide one simple interface to a set of interfaces in a subsystem.One NotificationFacade in front of e-mail, text and push services
StructuralDecoratorAttach extra responsibilities to an object at run time, as a flexible alternative to subclassing.Add logging or caching around a repository


One warning on Singleton: it creates global state, which makes classes harder to test alone. Use it for things that really exist once — the configuration — and nowhere else.


Nine patterns you will meet (2/2): behavioural
slide 31



FamilyPatternIntent, in one lineWhere in a campus app
BehaviouralObserverDefine a one-to-many dependency so that when one object changes state, all its dependants are informed and updated automatically.A report changes status → the reporter, the board and the statistics react
BehaviouralStrategyDefine a family of algorithms, put each one in its own class, and make them interchangeable for the code that uses them.Inform a reporter by e-mail or on a tracking page
BehaviouralCommandRepresent a request as an object, so that requests can be stored, queued, logged or undone.An “undo the last check-in” button in HabitHub


Observer and Strategy, in detail
slide 32



In Observer, the subject keeps a list of observers and offers attach() and detach(). When its state changes, it calls update() on each observer. The subject knows only that each observer has an update() method; it does not import the observers' classes. That is the low coupling of Lesson 1, built into a pattern: new observers can be added without editing the subject — the open–closed principle of Lesson 3.


In Strategy, a context object holds one strategy object. All strategies implement the same method, so the context calls it without asking which strategy it holds; adding a new strategy means adding a class, not editing an if/elif chain. The consequence to write down: each strategy is a class, so the number of classes grows, and the client must choose the right strategy somewhere — usually at creation time.


→ The figure of this lesson shows this part: Figure 4.


Choosing a pattern — and the pattern card
slide 33



Choose a pattern the way you choose a tool: from the problem. State the problem in one sentence from your requirements; find the patterns whose intent matches it; read their consequences; pick one, or none. A pattern added without a problem adds classes and indirection and solves nothing.


Record the choice on a pattern card, four lines: Problem — the sentence from your requirements; Pattern — its name and family; Where in our code — the classes that play each role; Consequences — what you gain and what you pay. One card is today's optional practice in the Studio, and the Mid-Term asks you to do exactly this on a new product: identify the pattern for a stated problem and sketch its classes.
🎯 Active break — Fun-quiz · 0:41–0:45 slide 36
Name that pattern — three scenarios
  1. Scenario 1: “The whole app must read one configuration object, created once.” Show 1 finger for Singleton, 2 for Factory Method, 3 for Adapter.
  2. Scenario 2: “When an order is marked ready, the student's screen and the kitchen statistics must both update — and the order class must not know them.” 1 Observer, 2 Command, 3 Facade.
  3. Scenario 3: “We must use a third-party campus-login library whose methods do not match the interface our controllers expect.” 1 Decorator, 2 Adapter, 3 Strategy.
  4. Thirty seconds per scenario: vote, then the answer in one sentence.
Check the answer
1 — Singleton (one instance, one access point). 2 — Observer (one-to-many notification; the subject does not know its observers). 3 — Adapter (convert an existing interface into the one the client expects).

Real-life example · Team Heron · SafeCampus (fictional)
SafeCampus: one status change, three reactions, two channels — Observer and Strategy
slide 34
TaskTeam Heron (fictional) builds SafeCampus: a student or a staff member reports a hazard — a broken stair light, a wet floor — under their name or anonymously, and follows its status until it is fixed. When a moderator changes the status of a report, three parts of the product must react, and a named reporter must be informed by e-mail while an anonymous one sees the update on a tracking page. The team chooses two patterns, implements them, and writes one pattern card for each.
Relation to the lectureIt applies Lesson 4: patterns chosen from problems, the roles of Observer and Strategy, and the consequences that go on the pattern card.
The problems. Problem 1: when a report changes status, the reporter must be informed, the security office's board must move the card, and — added later — the monthly statistics must count the fixed reports; the report class must not need to change each time a new reaction is added. Problem 2: the reporter is informed in one of two ways, e-mail for a named reporter and the tracking page for an anonymous one, and the code that informs must not contain an if/elif on anonymity.
The patterns. Problem 1 is Observer: HazardReport is the subject; ReporterUpdate, SecurityBoard and MonthlyStats are observers. Problem 2 is Strategy: each report holds one channel object, EmailChannel or TrackingPageChannel, and both offer the same send() method. When R-101 (named) and R-102 (anonymous) move to in progress, each report notifies its two observers, and the reporter message goes out through each report's own channel. MonthlyStats is then attached to R-101 without any change to HazardReport; when R-101 is fixed, three reactions run.
The cards. Observer — Problem: several parts react to a status change; the report must not know them. Where: HazardReport (subject), ReporterUpdate, SecurityBoard, MonthlyStats (observers). Consequences: + new reactions without editing the subject, + each observer testable with a fake report; − notifications run in the order of subscription, − one change triggers several calls, harder to follow when debugging. Strategy — Problem: two ways to inform, chosen per report. Where: HazardReport (context), EmailChannel and TrackingPageChannel (strategies). Consequences: + anonymity without a special case, + a text-message channel is one new class; − one more class per channel.
