# =============================================================================# CS 330 · Class 6 · Lesson 4 — Demo 4# SafeCampus (Team Heron, fictional): the Observer and Strategy patterns at work## TASK. Team Heron builds SafeCampus: a student or a staff member reports a hazard# on campus, under their name or anonymously, and follows its status until it is# fixed. When a report changes status, three parts of the product must react: the# reporter is informed, the security office's board moves the card, and the# monthly statistics are updated. The program implements this with the Observer# pattern (the report is the subject; the parts that react are observers that# subscribe to it) and the Strategy pattern (the way the reporter is informed is# an interchangeable object: an e-mail for a named reporter, a status line on a# tracking page for an anonymous one). It changes the status of two reports,# prints every notification, and then adds a new observer without editing the# report class.## RELATION TO THE LECTURE. Lesson 4: a design pattern is a problem, a solution and# its consequences. Observer answers "many parts must react to one change, and the# changed object must not know them"; Strategy answers "one task, several# interchangeable ways to do it, chosen at run time".## RUN IT: python3 demo4_safecampus_observer_strategy.py   (Python 3.8 or later, no extra package)# Educational material — Cyber.SoHo Educational Hub © 2026. All teams, products and people are fictional.# Use is governed by the Cyber.SoHo Legal Notice:# https://cyber-soho.github.io/prevmon/00.01.%20cyber.soho%20-%20legal.html# =============================================================================  # HazardReport is the SUBJECT of the Observer pattern: it keeps a list of observers and informs them of every change.class HazardReport:    # The constructor receives the tracking code of the report and the strategy chosen to inform its reporter.    def __init__(self, code, channel):        # The tracking code identifies the report, for example R-101.        self.code = code        # Every new report starts in the status "received".        self.status = "received"        # The channel is the STRATEGY object that knows how to reach this report's reporter.        self.channel = channel        # The list of subscribed observers starts empty; the report does not know their classes.        self.observers = []     # attach() subscribes an observer: any object that has an update(report) method.    def attach(self, observer):        # Add the observer at the end of the list.        self.observers.append(observer)     # set_status() changes the status and notifies every observer.    def set_status(self, new_status):        # Store the new status.        self.status = new_status        # Call update() on each subscribed observer, in the order they subscribed.        for observer in self.observers:            # Each observer decides on its own what the change means for it.            observer.update(self)  # EmailChannel is one STRATEGY for informing a reporter: an e-mail to a named reporter.class EmailChannel:    # send() delivers one message about one report.    def send(self, code, text):        # In a real product this would call an e-mail service; here the message is printed.        print(f"  e-mail -> reporter of {code}: {text}")  # TrackingPageChannel is another STRATEGY: an anonymous reporter sees the message on the tracking page of the code.class TrackingPageChannel:    # send() has the same signature as in EmailChannel, so the two strategies are interchangeable.    def send(self, code, text):        # Print the line that would appear on the anonymous tracking page; no personal data is involved.        print(f"  tracking page {code}: {text}")  # ReporterUpdate is an OBSERVER: it informs the reporter through the report's own strategy.class ReporterUpdate:    # update() is called by the subject after every status change.    def update(self, report):        # Delegate the delivery to the strategy stored in the report.        report.channel.send(report.code, f"your report is now '{report.status}'")  # SecurityBoard is an OBSERVER: the security office's board shows one card per report.class SecurityBoard:    # update() moves the card of the report to the column named after its status.    def update(self, report):        # Print the movement of the card.        print(f"  board  -> card {report.code} moves to column '{report.status}'")  # MonthlyStats is an OBSERVER added later, to count the reports that reach the status "fixed".class MonthlyStats:    # The constructor starts the counter at zero.    def __init__(self):        # fixed counts the reports fixed this month.        self.fixed = 0     # update() adds one to the counter when a report becomes "fixed".    def update(self, report):        # Only the status "fixed" matters to the statistics.        if report.status == "fixed":            # Increase the counter by one.            self.fixed += 1            # Print the new value of the counter.            print(f"  stats  -> fixed this month: {self.fixed}")  # Create the two observers that exist from the first release.reporter_update, board = ReporterUpdate(), SecurityBoard()# R-101 is a named report: its reporter is informed by e-mail.named = HazardReport("R-101", EmailChannel())# R-102 is anonymous: its reporter follows it on the tracking page.anonymous = HazardReport("R-102", TrackingPageChannel())# Subscribe both observers to both reports.for report in (named, anonymous):    # The reporter must be informed of every change.    report.attach(reporter_update)    # The security board must show every change.    report.attach(board) # A moderator starts work on the named report: both observers react, and the e-mail strategy is used.print("R-101 -> in progress")# Changing the status triggers the notifications.named.set_status("in progress")# The same change on the anonymous report uses the tracking-page strategy instead of e-mail.print("R-102 -> in progress")# Changing the status triggers the notifications.anonymous.set_status("in progress") # The statistics observer is added later; HazardReport is not edited (open for extension, closed for modification).stats = MonthlyStats()# Subscribe the new observer to the named report.named.attach(stats)# The named report is fixed: three observers now react.print("R-101 -> fixed")# Changing the status triggers the three notifications.named.set_status("fixed")# Print how many observers each report has at the end.print(f"observers: R-101 has {len(named.observers)}, R-102 has {len(anonymous.observers)}") # =============================================================================# STEP-BY-STEP EXPLANATION# 1. HazardReport is the subject. It stores its observers in a list and knows#    only one thing about them: each has an update(report) method. This is the#    low coupling the pattern buys: the report does not import the board or the#    statistics.# 2. EmailChannel and TrackingPageChannel are two strategies with the same#    send(code, text) method. The report holds one of them; the code that uses#    it never asks "which channel is this?" — no if/elif chain.# 3. ReporterUpdate, SecurityBoard and MonthlyStats are observers. Each one#    decides what a status change means for it.# 4. set_status("in progress") on R-101 calls two update() methods: the reporter#    receives an e-mail, the board moves the card. On R-102 the same code sends#    the message to the tracking page, because that report holds the other#    strategy: anonymity is kept without a special case.# 5. MonthlyStats is attached later. HazardReport is not modified, yet a third#    reaction appears when R-101 becomes "fixed": the class is open for#    extension and closed for modification (Lesson 3).# 6. Consequences, to write on the pattern card: + new reactions without#    editing the subject; + each observer can be tested alone with a fake#    report; - the order of notifications follows the order of subscription;#    - with many observers, one change triggers many calls, which is harder to#    follow when debugging.# =============================================================================

Live visualisation of the lecture idea
Step-by-step explanation
  1. HazardReport is the subject: it stores its status, its strategy object (channel) and a list of observers. attach() adds an observer; set_status() stores the new status and calls update() on every observer.
  2. EmailChannel and TrackingPageChannel are the two strategies. Both have the same send(code, text) method, so they can replace each other.
  3. ReporterUpdate, SecurityBoard and MonthlyStats are observers. Each one has an update(report) method and decides alone what a change means for it.
  4. R-101 holds the e-mail strategy, R-102 the tracking-page strategy. Both reports receive the same two observers.
  5. When R-101 and R-102 move to “in progress”, the visualisation lights up the arrows from the subject to its observers; the reporter message leaves through each report's own channel.
  6. MonthlyStats is attached later. HazardReport is not edited, yet the change to “fixed” now triggers three reactions. The last line prints 3 observers for R-101 and 2 for R-102.

Flash-cards
Five flash-cards for Lesson 4 — click a card to turn it
design patternclick to turn
A named description of a recurring design problem in a context, the core of its solution (classes, roles, collaboration) and the consequences of applying it. GoF (Gang of Four — Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides), 1994: 23 patterns.
the three families of GoF (Gang of Four — Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides) patternsclick to turn
Creational (how objects are created: Singleton, Factory Method, Builder), structural (how they are composed: Adapter, Facade, Decorator), behavioural (how they interact: Observer, Strategy, Command).
Observerclick to turn
One-to-many: when the subject changes state, it calls update() on every attached observer. The subject knows only the observer interface, so observers are added without editing it.
Strategyclick to turn
A family of interchangeable algorithms, each in its own class with the same method; the context holds one and calls it without asking which one it is — no if/elif on the kind.
pattern cardclick to turn
Four lines: Problem (from the requirements) → Pattern (name, family) → Where in our code (the classes in each role) → Consequences (what it gains, what it costs).

Lesson 5 — Frameworks and component-level design
0:45–0:56 · 11 minutes · slides 37–45
By the end of this lesson you can: Distinguish a framework from a library; choose a framework with a weighted criteria matrix; derive the operations of a design class diagram from a sequence diagram; read and draw a sequence diagram; state the three golden rules of interface design; compute fan-in and fan-out.
In full: Frameworks and component-level design: choosing a framework with a criteria matrix, the design class diagram and the sequence diagram, UI (User Interface) and UX (User Experience) basics — and the Numbers corner: fan-in, fan-out, coupling count


Framework or library?
slide 38



framework — A reusable, partly built application for one kind of software: it defines the structure, provides the common services, and calls the code that you write at the points it defines.


inversion of control — The property that separates a framework from a library: with a library, your code decides when to call it; with a framework, the framework decides when to call your code — for example, it calls your function when a browser requests a given web address.


Because a framework fixes the structure, choosing it is an architecture decision: changing it later means rewriting most of the product. Four frameworks cover most student teams. Flask↗ is a small Python web framework: you add only what you need. Django↗ is a complete Python framework with its own database layer — an ORM (Object–Relational Mapping) — authentication and an administration site. Express↗ is a minimal web framework for Node.js and JavaScript. Spring Boot↗ is the most used Java framework for web services. All four are free and open source; check the current version and its support period on the official site before you start, as the Lab 07 footnotes show.


Choosing a framework: the criteria matrix
slide 39



The method is the weighted matrix of Lesson 2, with criteria that matter for a framework. Team skills: how many members already write the language. Documentation: is there an official tutorial a beginner can follow? Testing support: does the framework come with a test client and work with a unit-test framework — pytest for Python, Jest for JavaScript, JUnit for Java? Fit: does its size match a product of 6 to 10 user stories? Community and support period: how active is it, and how long is the version you install supported?


For a four-week build, team skills usually weigh most: the best framework for a team that does not know its language is rarely the best framework for that team. The matrix, its weights and the decision go into an ADR (Architecture Decision Record), exactly like the architecture decision.


→ The figure of this lesson shows this part: Figure 5.


Component-level design and the design class diagram
slide 40



component-level design — The design of the inside of each component: its classes, their operations with parameters and types, their data structures and algorithms, and the interfaces through which it communicates — detailed enough to be coded directly.


design class diagram — A UML (Unified Modeling Language) class diagram that shows the classes of the solution, not only of the problem: the analysis classes of the domain model plus design classes (views, controllers, services, repositories, interfaces), with operations, visibility (+ public, − private) and types.


In Block 5 your domain model contained no screens, no controllers and no methods — those belonged to design. Now they arrive. Start from the domain model; add the design classes that the chosen architecture requires — a controller per feature, a service for the business rules, a repository per stored class; add the interfaces that your patterns and DIP (Dependency Inversion Principle) need. Where do the operations come from? From the sequence diagrams: every message that an object receives becomes an operation of its class. The UML (Unified Modeling Language) notation is defined by the OMG (Object Management Group) in the UML (Unified Modeling Language) 2.5.1 specification↗, and Mermaid or PlantUML can draw both diagrams from text inside your repository.


→ The figure of this lesson shows this part: Figure 5.


Sequence diagrams
slide 41



sequence diagram — A UML (Unified Modeling Language) interaction diagram that shows, for one scenario of one use case, the objects involved as vertical lifelines and the messages they exchange as horizontal arrows in time order, from top to bottom.


The elements are few. A lifeline is a box with the object's role and class, and a dashed vertical line below it. A synchronous message is a solid arrow with a filled head, labelled with the operation and its arguments; a return is a dashed arrow. A thin rectangle on a lifeline, an activation bar, shows that the object is busy. Conditions and repetitions go into labelled frames: alt for alternatives, opt for an optional part, loop for a repetition. Draw one diagram per important scenario — usually the main flow of each fully-dressed use case of Block 5 — and read it from top to bottom.


→ The figure of this lesson shows this part: Figure 5.


UI (User Interface) and UX (User Experience) basics: three golden rules
slide 42



user interface (UI (User Interface)) — The screens, controls, messages and other elements through which a person operates a product.


user experience (UX (User Experience)) — The person's overall perception and response before, during and after the use of a product — whether it is useful, easy and satisfying to use.


Interface design is the third layer of the design model. Your textbook, in chapter 12, uses the three golden rules of Theo Mandel (The Elements of User Interface Design, 1997). Place the user in control: no forced paths, an undo, interruptions allowed. Reduce the user's memory load: show the choices instead of asking the user to remember them, use defaults that make sense. Make the interface consistent: the same action looks and behaves the same everywhere in the product. Add the accessibility you met in Class 2: the W3C (World Wide Web Consortium)'s WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) 2.2↗ makes it testable — text alternatives for images, sufficient contrast, every function usable with a keyboard. The Nielsen Norman Group's ten usability heuristics↗ give a longer checklist for reviews.


Numbers corner: fan-in, fan-out and the coupling count
slide 43



fan-in — The number of different modules that call a given module (Sallie Henry and Dennis Kafura, 1981).


fan-out — The number of different modules that a given module calls.


Both are counted from a design, before any code exists: from the arrows of the sequence diagrams, or from the dependencies of the design class diagram. Henry and Kafura proposed them in Software structure metrics based on information flow↗. Read them together. A class with a high fan-in is reused by many others: good for reuse, and a reason to change it with care, because every change reaches all its callers. A class with a high fan-out depends on many others: it is harder to understand and harder to test alone, because each dependency must be replaced by a stub in a unit test. The coupling count of Lesson 1 is the fan-out measured on the dependencies of a class. The schedule's practical rule: a class with fan-out 9 and one method doing five things is the first thing to refactor.
✋ Active break — Try-it · 0:56–1:00 slide 46
A one-minute sequence diagram for “log in”, then one quiet minute
  1. One minute, on paper, alone: draw the sequence diagram of “log in” for your product — the user, the login view, the controller, the account repository. Number the messages; add the return arrows.
  2. One minute with a neighbour: is every arrow labelled with an operation? Which class has the largest fan-out?
  3. Last minute: one quiet minute — stand, stretch, breathe in for four counts and out for six. Nothing to do, on purpose.
  4. Keep the paper: the controller you drew is the first class of the code skeleton.
Check the answer
A minimal correct diagram: 1 User → LoginView: submit(email, password); 2 LoginView → LoginController: log_in(email, password); 3 LoginController → AccountRepository: find(email); 4 LoginController → LoginController: check(password) (a self-message); 5 LoginController → LoginView: show(home) — with dashed returns. The controller has the largest fan-out.

Real-life example · Team Lynx · StudyBuddy (fictional)
StudyBuddy: a framework matrix, one sequence diagram, and what its arrows say
slide 44
TaskTeam Lynx (fictional) builds StudyBuddy: a student finds study partners by course and sends a study request; the partner confirms or declines. The team chooses its framework with a weighted matrix, draws the sequence diagram of the main flow of “Send a study request”, derives from it the operations of its design class diagram, and counts the fan-in and fan-out of every class.
Relation to the lectureIt applies Lesson 5: framework selection with a criteria matrix, the sequence diagram, the design class diagram that it fills, and the Numbers corner.
The framework. Criteria and weights: team skills 30, documentation 20, testing support 20, fit for a small web app 20, community 10. Two members write Python, one writes JavaScript, none writes Java. Flask: (30×5 + 20×4 + 20×4 + 20×5 + 10×4) ÷ 100 = 4.50; Django 4.30 — excellent documentation and tests, but larger than the product needs; Express 4.00; Spring Boot 3.40. The team chooses Flask, with pytest for the unit tests of Block 7, and writes the matrix into its second ADR (Architecture Decision Record).
The sequence diagram. Eight numbered messages: the student presses Send on RequestView; the view submits to RequestController; the controller finds the classmate in StudentRepository, asks MatchPolicy whether the request is allowed — MatchPolicy reads the classmate's free windows from AvailabilityRepository — saves the request in RequestRepository with the status pending, asks Notifier to inform the classmate, and tells the view to show pending.
What the arrows say. Every arrow into an object becomes an operation of its class: find on StudentRepository, can_request on MatchPolicy, free_windows on AvailabilityRepository, save on RequestRepository, notify on Notifier, press_send and show on RequestView. RequestController has fan-in 1 and fan-out 5: it coordinates the use case, which is normal for a controller, but its unit test needs five stubs, and it is the class the team watches as features are added. The repositories have fan-out 0: they are the easiest classes to test.

"Django (Python)": {"team skills": 4, "documentation": 5, "testing support": 5, "fit for a small web app": 3, "community": 5},    # Express: a minimal web framework for Node.js; one member knows JavaScript.    "Express (JavaScript)": {"team skills": 3, "documentation": 4, "testing support": 4, "fit for a small web app": 5, "community": 5},    # Spring Boot: a Java framework; nobody in the team writes Java yet.    "Spring Boot (Java)": {"team skills": 1, "documentation": 5, "testing support": 5, "fit for a small web app": 3, "community": 5},# The closing brace ends the table of frameworks.}# Compute the weighted score of each framework: the sum of weight x score, divided by 100.totals = {name: sum(criteria[c] * s[c] for c in criteria) / 100 for name, s in frameworks.items()}# Print the frameworks from the best score to the worst.for name, total in sorted(totals.items(), key=lambda item: item[1], reverse=True):    # Show each framework with its score on the 1-to-5 scale.    print(f"framework {name:<21} {total:.2f}")# max() with key=totals.get returns the framework that has the highest score.choice = max(totals, key=totals.get)# Print the decision.print(f"decision: {choice}") # PART 2 — the sequence diagram of "Send a study request", one message per tuple: (sender, receiver, operation).messages = [    # The student, an actor outside the system, presses Send on the request form.    ("Student", "RequestView", "press_send(classmate, slot)"),    # The view passes the input to the controller of the request feature.    ("RequestView", "RequestController", "submit(classmate, slot)"),    # The controller loads the classmate's record.    ("RequestController", "StudentRepository", "find(classmate)"),    # The controller asks the matching policy whether the request is allowed.    ("RequestController", "MatchPolicy", "can_request(sender, classmate, slot)"),    # The policy reads the classmate's free time windows.    ("MatchPolicy", "AvailabilityRepository", "free_windows(classmate)"),    # The controller stores the new request with the status "pending".    ("RequestController", "RequestRepository", "save(request)"),    # The controller asks the notifier to inform the classmate.    ("RequestController", "Notifier", "notify(classmate, request)"),    # The controller tells the view to show the result to the student.    ("RequestController", "RequestView", "show(status='pending')"),# The closing bracket ends the list of messages.] # fan_in maps each class to the set of classes that send it messages; fan_out maps it to the classes it sends to.fan_in, fan_out = {}, {}# operations maps each class to the operations it must offer.operations = {}# Replay the messages in order, as they appear from top to bottom on the diagram.for number, (sender, receiver, operation) in enumerate(messages, start=1):    # Print the message with its number, the way it is labelled on the diagram.    print(f"{number}. {sender} -> {receiver}: {operation}")    # Every message received becomes an operation of the receiver's class: keep the name before the bracket.    operations.setdefault(receiver, set()).add(operation.split("(")[0])    # The actor is outside the system, so its messages are not counted in the fan metrics.    if sender == "Student":        # continue skips the counting for this message.        continue    # Record that the receiver receives a message from the sender.    fan_in.setdefault(receiver, set()).add(sender)    # Record that the sender sends a message to the receiver.    fan_out.setdefault(sender, set()).add(receiver) # The classes of the design: every class that sends or receives a message, except the actor.classes = sorted((set(fan_in) | set(fan_out) | set(operations)) - {"Student"})# Print one line per class with its operations, fan-in and fan-out.for cls in classes:    # The operations of the class, sorted alphabetically, joined into one text.    ops = ", ".join(sorted(operations.get(cls, set())))    # Print the class line; len() of an empty set is 0 for a class that never sends or never receives.    print(f"{cls:<22} fan-in {len(fan_in.get(cls, set()))} | fan-out {len(fan_out.get(cls, set()))} | operations: {ops}")# The class with the largest fan-out depends on the most other classes.busiest = max(classes, key=lambda cls: len(fan_out.get(cls, set())))# Print the result of the check.print(f"largest fan-out: {busiest} ({len(fan_out[busiest])}) - review it first if it keeps growing") # =============================================================================# STEP-BY-STEP EXPLANATION# 1. criteria and frameworks form a weighted criteria matrix. Flask:#    (30x5 + 20x4 + 20x4 + 20x5 + 10x4) / 100 = 4.50; Django 4.30; Express 4.00;#    Spring Boot 3.40. The weights state what matters to this team; with a#    Java-speaking team the same matrix would choose differently.# 2. messages is the sequence diagram written as data: one tuple per arrow,#    in the order of the diagram from top to bottom.# 3. For each message, the operation name before the bracket is added to the#    receiver: this is how a sequence diagram fills the design class diagram#    (RequestRepository gets save, MatchPolicy gets can_request, and so on).# 4. The actor Student is outside the system; its message creates the#    operation press_send of RequestView but is not counted in the fan sets.# 5. fan_in and fan_out are sets, so a class that sends two messages to the#    same class counts it once: RequestController sends to RequestView once.# 6. RequestController has fan-out 5: it coordinates the use case. That is#    expected for a controller, but it is also where growth is watched: a#    class whose fan-out keeps rising is the first candidate for a split.# 7. Repositories have fan-out 0 and fan-in 1: they are used, and use nothing.#    Low fan-out classes are easy to test alone; high fan-in classes are reused#    widely, so a change to them must be made with care.# =============================================================================

Live visualisation of the lecture idea
Step-by-step explanation
  1. criteria and frameworks form the weighted matrix. A dictionary comprehension computes all four totals in one line; sorted() prints them from best to worst, and max(totals, key=totals.get) picks Flask, 4.50.
  2. messages is the sequence diagram as data: one (sender, receiver, operation) tuple per arrow, in the order of the diagram.
  3. The loop replays the arrows one by one — watch the visualisation draw each one. For every message, the operation name before the bracket is added to the receiver's set of operations: the design class diagram fills up.
  4. The actor Student is outside the system: its message creates the operation press_send of RequestView, but continue skips the fan counting.
  5. fan_in and fan_out are dictionaries of sets, so a class counted twice is counted once. The class table prints fan-in, fan-out and operations for all seven classes.
  6. max() with a lambda finds RequestController, fan-out 5 — the class to review first if it keeps growing.

Flash-cards
Five flash-cards for Lesson 5 — click a card to turn it
framework vs libraryclick to turn
Your code calls a library when it needs it; a framework calls your code at the points it defines (inversion of control) and fixes the structure of the application — so choosing one is an architecture decision.
design class diagramclick to turn
The domain model plus design classes (views, controllers, services, repositories, interfaces), with operations, visibility and types; its operations come from the messages of the sequence diagrams.
sequence diagramclick to turn
One scenario of one use case: lifelines (vertical), numbered messages in time order (solid arrows), returns (dashed), activation bars, and frames such as alt, opt and loop.
the three golden rules of interface designclick to turn
Place the user in control; reduce the user's memory load; make the interface consistent (Theo Mandel, 1997; Pressman and Maxim, chapter 12). Plus accessibility: WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) 2.2.
fan-in and fan-outclick to turn
Fan-in: how many different classes call a class (reused → change with care). Fan-out: how many different classes it calls (depends on much → hard to test alone). Henry and Kafura, 1981.

Quiz — Lesson 5: 4 single-answer and 2 multiple-answer questions
FORMATIVE — practice only, NOT summative. This quiz does not count towards your grade; nothing you choose is recorded or sent anywhere.
Question 1 · MCQ (multiple-choice question — one correct answer)
What distinguishes a framework from a library?
Hint: Who calls whom?
Question 2 · MCQ (multiple-choice question — one correct answer)
Criteria weights: skills 30, documentation 20, testing 20, fit 20, community 10. A framework scores 2, 5, 5, 4, 5. What is its weighted score?
Hint: Multiply, add, divide by 100.
Question 3 · MCQ (multiple-choice question — one correct answer)
In a sequence diagram, message 6 is RequestController → RequestRepository: save(request). What does it add to the design class diagram?
Hint: An arrow into an object becomes…
Question 4 · MCQ (multiple-choice question — one correct answer)
A class is called by 6 different classes and calls 1 other class. What are its fan-in and fan-out?
Hint: Fan-in counts the callers; fan-out counts the callees.
Question 5 · MSQ (multiple-select question — several correct answers)
Which of these are Mandel's golden rules of interface design, or follow directly from them? (3 correct answers)
Hint: Control, memory, consistency.
Question 6 · MSQ (multiple-select question — several correct answers)
What do the numbers of the StudyBuddy example tell the team? (2 correct answers)
Hint: Fan-out 5 for the controller, fan-out 0 for the repositories.
